tasks.title: Write the TramCard component
tasks.description:
In `src/TramCard.jsx`, write a component called `TramCard` and export it by name. It takes three props, `number`, `name` and `built`, and returns: - an `
` with the class `tram-card` - inside it, an `

` with the tram's name - a `

` with the class `number` that reads `No. ` and the number, like `No. 14` - a `

` with the class `built` that reads `Built in ` and the year, like `Built in 1911` Everything on the card comes from its props. The check draws `TramCard` on its own with trams of its own.
nextSteps: Read "Props are the arguments of a component" in the lesson.
Copy the markup of one card from `App.jsx` into the return of `TramCard`.
Name the three props in the parameter list.
Replace each typed value with the prop it comes from.
hints: A card written by hand in `App.jsx` is the right markup. What changes is where its words come from.
React hands a component all its props as one object in the first parameter. Destructuring in the parameter list gives each prop its own name.
The function starts `export function TramCard({ number, name, built })`, and the card uses `{name}`, `{number}` and `{built}`.

tasks.title: One card for each tram
tasks.description:
In `src/App.jsx`, replace the three hand-written cards with three `TramCard` tags, one for each tram in `trams`, in the same order. Pass each one the tram's `number`, `name` and `built`. Keep the `div` with the class `trams` around them.

The check changes `trams.js` to trams of its own and reads the cards on the screen. It also asks React which component drew each card, so a card written by hand does not count.
nextSteps: Delete the first hand-written card and put a `TramCard` in its place.
Pass it the first tram's three values from `trams`.
Do the same for the other two, and compare the screen with `trams.js`.
hints: `trams` is an array. Its first tram is `trams[0]`.
A prop in quotes is text. A value from JavaScript goes in curly braces on the tag, and the prop names have to be the ones `TramCard` reads.
One card is `<TramCard number={trams[0].number} name={trams[0].name} built={trams[0].built} />`. Spreading `{...trams[0]}` passes the same three props.

tasks.title: Show what is between the tags
tasks.description:
Some trams need a line of their own. At the bottom of the card, `TramCard` has a `<div>` with the class `extra`, and inside it shows whatever is put between its opening and closing tags.

Then, in `App`, write the second card with an opening and a closing tag and the words `Out on the track today` between them.

The check puts an element of its own between the tags of a `TramCard`, then reads the second card on the screen.
nextSteps: Read "What goes between the tags" in the lesson.
Add the `extra` box at the bottom of the card.
Show what was put between the tags inside it.
Give the second card in `App` a closing tag and the words.
hints: What sits between a component's tags is passed to it like any other prop.
That prop always has the same name, and the component decides where it appears.

Add `children` to the props you take, and put `
{children}
` at the bottom of the card.

tasks.title: A status that falls back to On show
tasks.description:
Sometimes a tram is away for repair. `TramCard` takes one more prop, `status`, and shows it in a `

` with the class `status`. When no `status` is passed, the line reads `On show`. `App` passes no status today, so every card in the shed should say On show. The check draws the card once with a status of its own and once with none.
nextSteps: Read "A value to fall back on" in the lesson.
Take `status` as a prop and show it in a paragraph with the class `status`.
Look at the screen: the line is empty, because App passes no status.
Give `status` a default where you name it.
hints: A prop that nobody passes is `undefined`, and React shows nothing for it.
Destructuring can give a name a value to use when it is missing.
In the parameter list, write `status = 'On show'`.
